title: What If a Seaweed Belt Stretched Across the Atlantic?

scenes.text: What if a belt of seaweed drifted across the Atlantic? It does, and it keeps getting bigger.
In May 2025, scientists measured 38 million metric tons of sargassum, the most since records began in 2011.
The previous record was around 20 million tons, set in 2022.
It piles up from Puerto Rico to Guyana, and rotting seaweed gives off hydrogen sulfide, which smells like rotten eggs.
In Martinique, toxic gases forced a school to close, and on beaches it smothers sea turtle nests.
One researcher says the ocean may be shifting from seaweed-poor to seaweed-rich. The cause is still unproven.
